name: adjective agreement
title: Spanish Adjective Agreement Practice: Gender and Number Quiz
description: Practice Spanish noun-adjective agreement: -o and -a endings, adjectives in -e and consonants, plurals, mixed groups and nationalities, with 10 checked sentences.
answer: Spanish adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number. Adjectives in -o have four forms (alto, alta, altos, altas); adjectives in -e or most consonants have two (grande, grandes; fácil, fáciles). A mixed group of masculine and feminine nouns takes the masculine plural. Nationalities that end in a consonant add -a: español, española.

Mi padre y mi madre son altos.

rules.use: Z changes to c in the plural
rules.example: un niño feliz, unos niños felices

quiz.why: Consonant adjective in the plural: add -es, difíciles.

quiz.before: Mis tíos y mis tías son
quiz.why: A mixed group takes the masculine plural.
Nationalities in a consonant add -a: española.
Adjectives in -e do not change for gender.
Azul ends in a consonant: azules.
Two people: plural, and mixed or masculine takes -os.

mistakes: Matching the speaker instead of the noun: a man says «la casa es bonita», because casa is feminine.
Adding -a to adjectives in -e: «una chica inteligenta» should be «una chica inteligente».
Adding only -s to consonants: «fácils» should be «fáciles».
Using feminine plural for mixed groups: «los estudiantes (boys and girls) son simpáticos», not «simpáticas».
Forgetting that tricky nouns change the adjective: «el agua fría», «el problema serio», «la mano derecha».

heritage: Heritage speakers usually make adjectives agree by ear. In writing, the traps are tricky nouns like el agua (el agua está fría), el mapa and la foto, and English-style colors: in Spanish, colors agree when they are adjectives (camisas blancas) but not when a noun names the color (camisas color naranja).
teacher: Students describe a classmate with three adjectives without saying the name; the class guesses who it is. Then they describe two classmates together to practise plurals.

faq.question: Do all Spanish adjectives change for gender?
faq.answer: No. Adjectives ending in -o change (alto, alta). Most ending in -e, -ista or a consonant have one form for both genders (grande, optimista, fácil). Nationalities are the main exception: español, española.

faq.question: Which form do I use for a mixed group?
faq.answer: The masculine plural, even if there is only one masculine noun: mi madre, mis tías y mi tío son altos.

faq.question: Do adjectives always go after the noun?
faq.answer: Usually, but not always. Numbers, mucho, poco and a few others go before, and some adjectives change meaning by position: un gran amigo (a great friend), un amigo grande (a big friend).
